title: Why is learning to read hard?
author: Amy Coombe
summary: Opening with her sister's real childhood experience — a bright, language-rich child who still could not read after 975 hours of schooling built on 'read to her and give her lots of exposure to books,' but who learned within half a term once given explicit phonics teaching — this piece explains the cognitive science behind why reading must be directly taught rather than absorbed. Its core argument, drawn from Diane McGuinness and Maryanne Wolf, is that speech and reading are fundamentally different kinds of skills: humans have spoken for over 100,000 years and are biologically wired for it, while writing is a roughly 5,000-year-old human invention the brain never evolved to process, so it must repurpose existing systems (vision, language, motor coordination) through explicit instruction. The author uses the analogy of walking versus riding a bike to make this concrete — one develops through natural exposure, the other requires being taught — and argues reading works the same way as the bike. She breaks down the specific 'code-breaking' demands of reading an alphabetic script: understanding that writing represents speech, segmenting spoken words into individual sounds, and mapping those sounds onto letters, noting that hearing individual speech sounds in words is itself not something humans are biologically primed to do. Aimed explicitly at secondary reading leads without time to study reading science in depth, the piece's practical payoff is a warning against the 'dangerous pitfall' of assuming struggling readers will improve through more exposure alone, when what they need is direct, explicit teaching.

quotes: Yet, after one full year of schooling — 975 hours of teaching — and hours of support at home, Laura had still not learned to read.
She was quickly given extra reading lessons, and within a half term of explicit phonics teaching, Laura had learned to read.
The answer begins with a simple truth: speaking and reading are two fundamentally different things. We are born ready to speak, but not ready to read.

Unlike with spoken language, the brain didn’t evolve to read and write. Reading requires the brain to use existing systems that evolved for other purposes, getting them to work together in different ways.
We could give a child a bike but they’re highly unlikely to learn through exposure alone. They need to be taught. It’s just the same with reading.
Segmenting speech in this way is a significant obstacle in learning to read and spell because hearing individual speech sounds in words is not something we’re biologically programmed to do.

Having some knowledge of the difficulty of learning to read will help us avoid a dangerous pitfall: assuming that children who’ve not yet learned to read will get better simply through more exposure to reading.
